title: For such a time (Esther 4:14)
hook: a Jewish queen risks her life for her people; Jews keep Purim remembering it
carry: for such a time as this

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fall of Jerusalem, and your line was even exile is not the end.

Far from Jerusalem, in the Persian royal city of Shushan, Jews are still scattered across the empire. A young Jewish woman, Esther, raised by her cousin Mordecai, has become queen, and she has kept quiet about who her people are. Then a powerful official, Haman, angry that Mordecai won't bow to him, gets the king to sign an order to destroy the Jews of the whole empire on a single day. He picks the day by casting lots. Mordecai sends word to the palace: go to the king. Esther sends word back: anyone who walks in uncalled is put to death, unless the king holds out his golden scepter.
screen: `GO IN UNCALLED, AND YOU MAY DIE.`

segments.voice: Mordecai doesn't flatter her. The palace won't hide her, he says, and then: "For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place." Help will come from somewhere; will she be part of it? Then: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" He doesn't claim to be sure. He asks her to consider that her strange place, a Jewish orphan in a Persian crown, might not be an accident. Esther asks the Jews of the city to fast for her three days, and she and her maids will fast too. Then: "so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish." She goes in. The king holds out the scepter. In a reversal, Haman ends up on the gallows he built for Mordecai, and the Jews are allowed to defend themselves. "They called these days Purim after the name of Pur," and Pur, the text says, means the lot Haman cast. The book asks for days of feasting and joy, sending portions to one another and gifts to the poor, and Jewish tradition keeps Purim by reading the scroll of Esther aloud. Some readers point out that in this book, as the King James Bible prints it, God is never named. Yet Jewish and Christian readers have long heard God at work behind it, through a cousin's question and a queen's nerve.

Think of a place where you have access others don't, a boss who listens, a family group chat, a friend who trusts you, where one true word could help someone who can't get in the room. Notice what keeps you quiet, fear or comfort, without deciding anything yet. If you pray, bring that door to God; if you don't, just stand in front of it for a while.
Purim. The festival named for the lot Haman cast, kept by Jews to remember how Esther went in to the king and her people were saved.
Your line: for such a time as this. Who knows what your place is for. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians read Esther as scripture and sometimes quote Mordecai's for such a time as this when someone takes on a hard calling; Jews keep Purim each year by reading the scroll of Esther aloud, sending food to friends and giving gifts to the poor.

notes: Purim customs (reading the Megillah aloud, noise at Haman's name, mishloach manot, gifts to the poor) described briefly as a neighbor's practice; Esther 9:22 names portions and gifts to the poor. A Jewish reviewer may wish to confirm the description.

'In Esther as the King James Bible prints it, God is never named' refers to the Hebrew-based book; the Greek additions (in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, and the KJV Apocrypha) do name God. Confirm wording, and whether to mention the Greek additions for this broad path.
'Readers, Jewish and Christian, have heard God all through it' is interpretive; confirm.

The reversal (Haman hanged on the gallows built for Mordecai, Jews permitted to defend themselves) summarizes 7:10 and 8:11; the violence of chapter 9 is not described. Confirm the summary is acceptable.
